title: six words
hookLine: six words; the sentence a Jew says with eyes covered

lines: THE FIRST PRAYER AND THE LAST.
cards: A synagogue on an ordinary morning. People are reading, murmuring, some standing, some swaying. Then, at one moment, many of them do the same small thing.
They raise a hand and cover their eyes. For a few seconds a room full of adults sits like children playing hide and seek. And under the hands, six Hebrew words.

Some children learn it as their first prayer, at bedtime, and tradition hopes it will be among the last words a person says in this life. Six words, said at the beginning and the end. Today: the sentence under the hand.

teach.h: SHEMA — HEAR, LISTEN, TAKE IT IN.
teach.b: The six words are: Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad.

teach.h: SAID TO ISRAEL, NOT TO GOD.
teach.b: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." They come from the Torah, from the same passage that's rolled up inside the mezuzah, and the prayer is named for its first word. Shema.
Hear. But the Hebrew verb is bigger than hearing with your ears. It means listen, pay attention, understand, even take it to heart and act on it.
It's not here is a fact. It's are you listening? Notice who it's said to.
Not to God. To Israel, to the people, to the person saying it. It's a sentence you say to yourself, out loud, to wake yourself up.
A detail about the name. The word written there is God's four-letter name, which Jewish tradition doesn't pronounce. Reading aloud, people say Adonai, my Lord, instead.
And a detail about the page. In a handwritten Torah scroll, two letters in this verse are written extra large: the last letter of the first word and the last letter of the last word.
Together they spell ed, the Hebrew word for witness. Saying it, some teachers say, is a kind of testimony.

teach.h: A HAND OVER THE EYES, TO HEAR.
teach.b: Why the hand over the eyes? An old story remembers that Rabbi Judah the Prince, whom tradition credits with gathering the rabbis' early teachings into one book, passed his hand over his eyes when he said it.
People still do: shut out everything you can see, just for a moment, so you can hear. The same passage says to speak these words when you lie down and when you rise up.
So it's said morning and night, at bedtime, and at the end.

how: Jews traditionally say the Shema in the morning and evening prayers and again at bedtime, covering the eyes with the right hand for the first line; some parents say it with their children as they fall asleep.

games.q: what's inside the six words — tap the pairs.
p: said in place of God's name

s: the Shema is spoken to God
it's spoken to Israel, to the people and to yourself: hear.
the Shema is the passage inside a mezuzah
the same words from the Torah are rolled up in the case on the doorpost.
covering the eyes is a modern custom
an old story remembers Rabbi Judah the Prince doing it.

games.q: you're Rabbi Judah the Prince, about to say the Shema in a busy room. what do you do?
o: say it louder than everyone else.
pass your hand over your eyes.
stand up and face the door.
games.why: the Talmud remembers him passing his hand over his eyes. shut out what you can see, so you can hear.

practice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Cover your eyes with one hand, the way people do for the Shema. Let the room disappear.
Breathe slowly and just listen, to whatever sound is left: a fan, traffic, your own breath. If you pray, you can say the six words on the way out. If not, let the breath out and simply hear.

wordCard.voice: The Shema. Six words that begin hear, O Israel, said morning and night with the eyes covered. Thirteenth word.

orig.note: Hebrew: hear, and also listen, understand, take to heart.

carryVoice: Your line: hear. Not only with the ears: listen, and take it in. Day thirteen.
